newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - OPEC, Iraq may yield to numbers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - OPEC, Iraq may yield to numbers.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices were expected to moderate this week despite the possible threat of market moving developments from the mid-year OPEC meeting, and heightened diplomatic tensions between Iraq and the U.N.

Basic fundamentals could win out over the newsier sectors of the trade for market attention. Traders said one candidate for pushing out OPEC/Iraq dominance are weekly American Petroleum Institute (API) numbers.
"We could see a little support from the API's, even if it shows moderation from recent numbers, with modest draws in gasoline or crude," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
The trader saw August NYMEX screen prices ranging from $18.75-19.25 a barrel for the week, a relatively tight trading band indicative of a possible restful market.

A key question on traders minds remains when Iraq crude will return to market. Guessing the date when new oil sales contracts will be signed and liftings resumed has become part of the daily routine. Best information from the U.N. pegs new sales around early to mid-July, though many traders think the date will be later in the summer.

As it stands now, Baghdad has yet to complete its version of the aid distribution plan necessary for restarting the oil sales side of the renewed "oil-for-food" accord. U.N. officials must receive the plan for review and approval before sales can start. A pricing formula must also be submitted by Iraq.
Monday, a senior U.N. aid official said Iraq was at least one week away from finishing the aid plan.

Traders are suspicious of Iraqi motives, thinking Baghdad may hold back oil sales as a tit-for-tat type move to protest U.S. blocks on food and medicine contracts. Just last week, a top Iraqi official in New York said the $800 million sitting in an escrow account from first round oil sales must be exhausted before new sales start.

Stormy clouds on the separate issue of weapons inspections in Iraq came to the forefront over the weekend. A little arm-twisting by U.S. President Bill Clinton at the Denver summit won Russian approval for a stern U.N. Security Council warning to Baghdad.

The council unanimously approved an American and British plan telling Iraq to comply with U.N. inspectors, or else face even stiffer sanctions. The council also threw out the regular 60-day review on sanctions, delaying the next such report until October.

The news agenda from OPEC, and its semi-annual meeting in Vienna, may have less of an impact on the market that in recent times. Traders said the fact OPEC cheating on quota ceilings has been well-established lends a certain immunity to headline buying and selling.
"The market is jaded by OPEC. It isn't as meaningful as in the past," said Brown, who noted there is still the possibility for a market jolt if an extremely sensitive, or suprising statement emerges.
Most market traders expect a short meeting, with member approval for a quota rollover at the current 25.033 million barrels per day (bpd) ceiling.
On the domestic cash market front, all eyes are focused on word of how much, if any, foreign crude was delivered against the July NYMEX contract on expiry day last Friday.
For at least a week, markets were abuzz with word U.S. refiners were buying foreign overhang -- mainly Nigerian Bonny Light crude -- soaking-up the amount of deliverable crude.

July Exchange for Physicals (EFPs) had crept down to only a few pennies over the NYMEX screen value by the time Friday business ended. The lower the chance for foreign crude deliveries, the weaker the EFP premium, traders noted.

When May and June NYMEX contracts expired, 2.73 million barrels and 2.349 million barrels of foreigns were delivered against contracts, scaring refiners and trade houses fearful of getting stuck with uneconomical supply.
Bonny Light receivers, for instance, must pay a premium to the delivering party of some 40 cents per barrel from July 1.
